procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders passed by the National Commission adjourning matters along with interlocutory applications awaiting appropriate orders in a writ petition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a writ petition (C.W.P. No. 34595 of 2019) in the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh. The High Court directed the Registrar General, Haryana to decide the interim applications expeditiously (order dated 27.11.2019).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by filing Civil Appeal No. 4718 of 2022 and Civil Appeal Nos. 329-332 of 2023 seeking to set aside the orders passed by the National Commission. The appellant argues that the pendency of the writ petition has no connection with the proceedings before the National Commission and that the National Commission erred in adjourning the matters sine die.

directions: The impugned orders are set aside.
Pending applications, if any, are disposed of.
The National Commission shall proceed to hear the matters on merits, expeditiously.

issue.issue_text: Whether the National Commission was justified in adjourning the consumer complaints sine die to await the outcome of a writ petition pending before the High Court, especially when no stay was granted by the High Court.

facts: An association of allottees filed several consumer complaints in 2017 before the National Commission.
A separate legal dispute arose concerning the registration and byelaws of the appellant association, which was challenged in a writ petition before the High Court.
The National Commission was informed of this pending writ petition and, as a result, adjourned the consumer complaints sine die (indefinitely) to await its outcome.
Crucially, the High Court had not granted any stay order in the writ petition that would have prevented the National Commission from proceeding.
law: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, a 'complainant' can include multiple consumers filing a joint complaint (Section 12(1)(a)).
application: The Supreme Court found that the issue of the association's registration, which was the subject of the writ petition, had "no relevancy" to the merits of the consumer complaints.

The Court reasoned that since individual affidavits had been filed by the allottees, their complaints could be treated as joint complaints filed by individual consumers under Section 12(1)(a) of the Act.
Therefore, the validity of the association's registration was not a barrier to adjudicating the complaints.
The Court criticized the National Commission for adopting a "pedantic and hyper-technical approach" that resulted in the cases not progressing for over five years.
The absence of a stay order from the High Court further weakened the justification for the adjournment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the National Commission was not justified in adjourning the consumer complaints sine die. The pendency of the writ petition regarding the association's registration was irrelevant to the substance of the consumer complaints, especially since individual allottees had filed affidavits and the High Court had not issued a stay. The Court set aside the National Commission's order to allow the long-pending complaints to be adjudicated on their merits.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the National Commission was justified in adjourning the consumer complaints sine die to await the outcome of a writ petition pending before the High Court, especially when no stay was granted by the High Court.
appellant_arguments: The respondent is deliberately trying to prevent the appellant from seeking a legal remedy, causing significant delays in complaints filed in 2017.
The writ petition pending in the High Court is not connected to the proceedings before the National Commission.
The National Commission erred in adjourning the matters sine die, particularly since individual allottees had already filed their affidavits.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Consumer Protection Act is a social benefit-oriented legislation, and therefore, courts must adopt a constructive and liberal approach when construing its provisions.
obiter: The Preamble of the Act, which uses the word 'protection', can provide useful assistance in ascertaining legislative intent, but it cannot control the otherwise plain meaning of a provision.
The law addresses the need to protect the common person from wrongs for which remedies under ordinary law have become illusory, as enforcement machinery is often ineffective or inefficient.

legal_tests_applied: The provisions of the Consumer Protection Act must be construed using a constructive liberal approach in favour of the consumer to achieve the purpose of the enactment, as it is a social benefit-oriented legislation.
policy_considerations: The Act, 1986 is a social benefit-oriented legislation and, therefore, the Court has to adopt a constructive liberal approach while construing the provisions of the Act.
The Act was enacted to provide for the protection of the interests of consumers, and the use of the word 'protection' furnishes the key to the minds of the makers of the Act.
The law meets a long-felt necessity of protecting the common man from wrongs for which the remedy under ordinary law has, for various reasons, become illusory.

The primary duty of the Court/Commission while construing the provisions of such an Act is to adopt a constructive approach, provided it does not do violence to the language of the provisions and is not contrary to the attempted objective of the enactment.
